script.opening: (Mother, Aria on her lap, holding up her phone; apologetic.) "Aria's right eye turns inwards sometimes, especially when she's tired. My mum says all babies do it and she'll grow out of it. But the thing that's actually been bothering me — in a few flash photos lately, that same eye looks white in the middle, not red like the other one. Is that anything, or am I being daft?"

facts.text: "Here, this one from last week. See, her left eye is red but the right one is sort of white" — holds the phone to the camera. "Three or four photos. I'm not sure I've seen it otherwise." Over the last month.
"It comes and goes. I honestly can't say exactly when it started" — noticed for about 2 months; more when tired. Was never there as a young baby as far as she knows.
"Nothing I've noticed. She plays normally." Doesn't bump into things. If asked: she sometimes tilts her head to look at books.
"No, none of that. She's herself" — no red or painful eye, no swelling, no rubbing, eating and sleeping well, no fevers.
"Not that I know of" — no eye cancers, childhood cataracts or squints in the family. Aria's dad wore glasses as a child.
Born at term, healthy. Newborn and 6–8 week checks normal. Immunisations up to date. No medicines, no allergies.
Lives with Mum (Abena, nurse in a care home) and Dad (works away). Can bring her to the surgery this afternoon.
"I googled it and scared myself. Then my mum said I'm overreacting and I felt silly for booking."

Apologetic and anxious. Wants to know: "Tell me if it matters, I suppose." If the word tumour or cancer is mentioned, go quiet: "(quietly) A tumour… in her eye?" Then practical: "Today? Yes, I can bring her this afternoon." If told she'll grow out of it, look relieved but unconvinced (the trap).

ice.ideas: (Grandmother) "She'll grow out of it." (Mother) "The white in the photos might be something."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she googled the white reflex and saw "eye cancer"; frightened but worried she's overreacting.
ice.expectations: "To know if the white in the photos matters."

cues: "Am I being daft?" — validate her instinct.
"Looks white in the middle." — leukocoria; the key red flag.
"I googled it and scared myself." — her fear to acknowledge.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the WHITE reflex (LEUKOCORIA) in photos / an absent or abnormal RED REFLEX as a serious RED FLAG for RETINOBLASTOMA (and cataract/other pathology) — taking the parental report extremely seriously, never "grow out of it"

Applies NICE NG12: an absent fundal (red) reflex / suspected retinoblastoma in a child → consider a suspected cancer pathway referral to ophthalmology; and NICE NG127: a new-onset squint with loss of the red reflex → immediate ophthalmology referral — and makes the referral

Arranges a same-day face-to-face EXAMINATION of the red reflex in both eyes (priority; not possible on video), plus corneal light reflex/cover test for the squint and visual fixation, and asks to SEE the photographs

Assesses the SQUINT appropriately — recognising that a constant squint, any squint after about 3 months of age, or one with reduced vision risks AMBLYOPIA and needs orthoptic/ophthalmology referral, so "grow out of it" is not a safe blanket reassurance

Refers and acts without delay — NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway referral for the leukocoria/retinoblastoma (immediate referral under NICE NG127 if a new squint with loss of the red reflex) plus orthoptic/paediatric ophthalmology for the squint/amblyopia — not watch-and-wait
Validates the mother’s instinct (right to mention the photos), explains honestly why urgent assessment is needed WITHOUT inducing panic, and avoids both false reassurance and catastrophic language
Supports an anxious parent through the urgent referral, acknowledges most squints are benign while the white reflex specifically needs prompt checking, and checks understanding

Safety-nets and follows up: the urgent referral made today, what to do meanwhile, the squint/amblyopia pathway, confirmation of attendance, and parental support — prompt NICE NG12/NG127 action for leukocoria, not dismissal

worked.txt: "You are absolutely not being daft — you’ve spotted something really important. A white look in one eye in flash photos is exactly the kind of thing we want to know about, and I’m glad you mentioned it. Could I see those photos?"

"I need to check what we call the ‘red reflex’ in both her eyes — the red glow you normally get — and I can’t do that properly over video, so I’d like to see Aria in person today. … I want to compare them carefully, because if one looks white or absent, that needs an urgent specialist look."

"Most of the time a turning eye is harmless and treatable. But a white reflex specifically can be a sign of a problem at the back of the eye that we never sit on — occasionally it can be something serious, so the safe thing is a quick urgent assessment by the eye specialists."

"I’m going to refer Aria urgently to the eye specialists to be seen very soon — within hours if the check shows the reflex is lost alongside the turning eye — this is the right, careful thing to do, not an overreaction. They’ll examine the back of the eye properly."

"Separately, the turning-in eye also needs the orthoptic/eye team, because if a squint sticks around it can make that eye lazy, and treating it early protects her vision. The urgent referral will cover her eyes fully."

"I know this is frightening — it’s a precaution because you were observant. I’ll make sure the appointment comes through quickly and follow it up. If you notice the white reflex more, or any change in her eye, tell us. You did exactly the right thing."

f.learning: In a young child, a WHITE reflex (LEUKOCORIA) — including one a parent notices in flash PHOTOGRAPHS — or an ABSENT/abnormal RED REFLEX on examination is a serious RED FLAG that can indicate RETINOBLASTOMA (a malignant eye tumour of early childhood), as well as congenital cataract or other pathology, and must never be dismissed as "she’ll grow out of it". NICE NG12 (children and young people) advises considering a suspected cancer pathway referral to ophthalmology for retinoblastoma in a child with an absent fundal (red) reflex, and NICE NG127 advises immediate referral (seen within hours) for a new-onset squint with loss of the red reflex, so examine the red reflex in both eyes face to face the same day (compare for an absent, white or asymmetric reflex — not possible on video), ask to see the photographs the parent describes, and make that urgent referral — a credible parental report of leukocoria warrants referral even if the in-clinic reflex looks equivocal. Separately, assess the SQUINT (strabismus): intermittent squint in the first ~3 months of life can be normal, but a constant squint, any squint after about 3 months of age, a squint with reduced vision, or any concern needs orthoptic/ophthalmology referral, because untreated squint risks AMBLYOPIA ("lazy eye") and permanent vision loss if not treated early — so "they’ll grow out of it" is not a safe blanket reassurance. Refer and act without delay (NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026) suspected cancer pathway referral for the leukocoria/retinoblastoma, or immediate referral under NICE NG127 for a new squint with loss of the red reflex, plus orthoptic/paediatric ophthalmology for the squint), and communicate by validating the parent’s instinct, explaining honestly why urgent assessment is needed without inducing panic, acknowledging that most squints are benign while the white reflex specifically needs prompt checking, and supporting an anxious parent — avoiding both false reassurance and catastrophic language.

knowledge.guideline: [2] NICE NG127 Suspected neurological conditions: recognition and referral (2019), children: new-onset squint · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [3] NHS Newborn and Infant Physical Examination (NIPE) screening programme: eye examination at birth and 6 to 8 weeks · [4] UK National Screening Committee: child vision screening (orthoptist-led, age 4 to 5)
knowledge.summary: A white pupil in flash photographs (leukocoria) in a toddler is a retinoblastoma warning sign until an eye specialist says otherwise. Take the mother’s observation seriously, look at the photos, arrange for the red reflex to be checked face to face, and refer to ophthalmology: an absent fundal reflex needs a suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12), and a new squint with loss of the red reflex needs an immediate referral (NG127). The squint needs specialist assessment in its own right because of the amblyopia risk. “She’ll grow out of it” is not safe advice here.

points.t: A white, pale or “cat’s eye” reflection in one pupil on flash photos, or an absent or abnormal red reflex on examination, can be caused by retinoblastoma, congenital cataract, Coats’ disease or other serious eye disease. Parents often notice it in photos first. The report alone is enough to act on.

NICE NG12 [1]: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral to ophthalmology for retinoblastoma in a child with an absent fundal (“red”) reflex. NICE NG12 now says “fundal” reflex because the normal reflex can look a different colour in children with darker skin.

points.h: NG127: squint plus loss of red reflex
points.t: NICE NG127 [2]: refer immediately to ophthalmology a child with a new-onset squint together with loss of the fundal (“red”) reflex in one or both eyes (seen within a few hours). It can signal retinoblastoma, other progressive eye disease or raised intracranial pressure. A new squint with headache, vomiting or ataxia needs immediate referral to acute paediatrics.

A persisting squint in a toddler is not something to wait on: the brain can suppress the turning eye and amblyopia (“lazy eye”) develops, which responds best to early glasses, patching or other treatment. In UK practice any squint beyond early infancy (about 3 months of age) is referred for orthoptic and ophthalmology assessment. A squint can also be the first sign of poor vision in that eye, including from retinoblastoma.

Face to face: red reflex of each eye separately and then both together from about an arm’s length in a dim room, comparing colour, brightness and symmetry; corneal light reflex and cover test; fixing and following; eyelids and pupils. On video: look at the photos, watch for the turn, and ask about vision, headache, vomiting and unsteadiness.

The red reflex is checked at the newborn and 6 to 8 week NIPE examinations [3], and orthoptist-led vision screening happens at 4 to 5 years [4]. A normal baby check does not rule out later disease, so a new parental concern overrides earlier reassurance.

Validate the mother’s instinct, explain honestly that the white reflex is the reason for urgency, say that most causes are not cancer but that this must be checked quickly, and avoid both false reassurance and frightening language. Confirm she knows when and where Aria will be seen.

Family pressure (“she’ll grow out of it”), who can support the mother, practical barriers to attending today.
Asked to see the photos; arranged face-to-face red reflex, corneal light reflex and cover test, fixation and following.
Retinoblastoma, congenital cataract and other retinal disease versus benign squint; amblyopia risk.
Asked about headache, vomiting, unsteadiness, drowsiness, eye pain or redness, reduced vision and family history.
Named leukocoria as a warning sign needing urgent specialist eye assessment; explained the squint risk.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Same-day phone call to ophthalmology; NG127 immediate if new squint with loss of red reflex, otherwise NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway referral; squint assessed by the same team.
Supported the mother, offered support for attending, helped her explain the plan to the family.
Teach-back; chase if no appointment in a few days; red flags for same-day review; practice confirms attendance.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.

Idea (grandmother: normal), concern (a tumour after searching online, fear of overreacting), expectation (to know if it matters).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.

When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Osei. Can you hear and see me all right? And is that Aria with you? Tell me what’s been happening.
model.why: Checks the video link and opens openly

model.text: (Mother) Yes, she’s on my lap. Her right eye turns inwards sometimes, mostly when she’s tired. My mum says all babies do it and she’ll grow out of it. But what’s been bothering me is that in a few flash photos that same eye looks white in the middle, not red like the other one. Is that anything, or am I being daft?
You’re not being daft at all. You’ve mentioned two things, the eye turning in and the white look in photos, and I want to go through both properly. Is that all right?
model.why: Names both problems and agrees the agenda

model.text: Yes, please.
Let’s start with the photos. Could you show me one on your screen, or send it through to the practice?
Here, this one from last week. See, her left eye is red but the right one is sort of white.
Thank you, that’s really helpful. I can see what you mean. How many photos show it, and do you ever notice it in normal light, for example a pale glint in her eye?
model.why: Clarifies how often and whether it is seen outside photos

model.text: Three or four photos. I’m not sure I’ve seen it otherwise.
And the turning in: when did you first notice it, and is it there all the time or does it come and go?
model.why: Onset and pattern of the squint

model.text: It comes and goes. I honestly can’t say exactly when it started.
That’s fine. Does she seem to see well? For example, does she bump into things on one side, tilt her head, or get upset if you cover one eye?
Nothing I’ve noticed. She plays normally.
Has she had headaches, been sick in the mornings, been unsteady on her feet or more sleepy than usual? Any redness, pain or a change in the size of the eye?
model.why: Screens for NG127 features and other eye disease

model.text: No, none of that. She’s herself.
Has anyone in the family had an eye problem as a child, or had an eye removed or treated for a tumour?
Not that I know of.
When you saw that white eye in the photo, what went through your mind?
model.why: Explores the mother’s idea and fear

model.text: I googled it and scared myself. Then my mum said I’m overreacting and I felt silly for booking.
You did exactly the right thing booking. Noticing that in a photo is often how these things are found, and I’m glad you didn’t leave it. What were you hoping I could do today?
model.why: Validates her instinct and asks her expectation

model.text: Tell me if it matters, I suppose.

It does matter, and I’ll be honest with you. The white look means light isn’t bouncing back off the back of that eye in the normal way. Most of the time that turns out to be something like a cloudy lens or another eye condition that can be treated, but occasionally it’s a rare eye tumour called retinoblastoma. That’s why we never wait on it. Eye specialists need to look at the back of her eye soon.
model.why: Explains leukocoria honestly, names the serious cause without catastrophising

model.text: (quietly) A tumour… in her eye?

I know that’s a frightening word to hear. I’m not saying she has it. I’m saying it needs to be ruled out quickly, and if it were found, it’s one of the childhood cancers that’s treated most successfully when it’s caught early. Checking quickly is the careful thing to do.
model.why: Responds to distress with honesty and hope

model.text: Okay. And the turning eye?

The squint needs the specialists too. If an eye keeps turning, the brain can start ignoring it and it becomes a lazy eye, which is much easier to treat when she’s young. So “she’ll grow out of it” isn’t safe for Aria. The same eye team can look at both.
model.why: Explains amblyopia risk and why the squint needs referral

model.text: I can’t check the red reflex properly over video, so I’d like to see her in person today, in a dim room with my ophthalmoscope. I’ll also phone the eye doctors at the hospital today. If the reflex is missing in that eye with the squint, they’ll want to see her within hours. Otherwise I’ll send an urgent referral on the fast-track pathway for suspected eye cancer, which means an appointment within two weeks. Either way, the referral goes today.
model.why: Face-to-face red reflex, same-day ophthalmology discussion, NG127 immediate or NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway

model.text: Today? Yes, I can bring her this afternoon.
Good, we’ll book a time this afternoon. Please bring the photos on your phone, because the specialists find them helpful. Would it help to have someone with you?
I’ll see who can come with me.
Good. Is there anything you’d like me to say differently to your mum? Some families find it helps to hear that the doctor asked for this, not that you overreacted.
Yes. I’ll tell her the doctor said it needs checking.
Can you tell me in your own words what we’ve agreed, so I know I’ve explained it well?
Bring her in this afternoon to check the red reflex and bring the photos. You’ll ring the eye doctors today, and she’ll be seen either very quickly or within two weeks. The squint gets checked too.

That’s exactly right. If you haven’t heard about the eye appointment within a few days, ring me and I’ll chase it. Before then, if she gets headaches, morning vomiting, becomes unsteady or drowsy, or the eye becomes red, painful or looks bigger, call us straight away or take her to A&E. I’ll also check with the hospital that she was seen.
model.why: Timed follow-up, specific safety-net and ownership of the referral

social.t: Relatives saying “she’ll grow out of it” can make a parent doubt herself. Give her words to use at home and credit her for noticing.
Urgent eye appointments may be at a specialist centre some distance away. Ask about transport, childcare and work, and signpost support.

legal.t: A person with parental responsibility consents to examination and referral for a 2-year-old. Record who attended and what was agreed.
If an essential examination such as the red reflex cannot be done on video, arrange it face to face promptly rather than deferring the decision.

professional.t: Safety-net properly: confirm the referral was received and the child was seen. Missed or delayed suspected cancer referrals in children are a recognised source of harm.
NICE NG12 asks clinicians to take persistent parental concern seriously and consider referral. Here there is a specific red flag as well.

community.t: The Childhood Eye Cancer Trust (CHECT) gives family information on retinoblastoma. Health visitors can support follow-up and later orthoptic care.

redFlags: White or absent red reflex, including in flash photos
New squint with loss of the red reflex (NG127: immediate referral)
New squint with headache, vomiting or unsteadiness (immediate paediatric referral)
Reduced vision, a painful red eye or a change in eye size
psychosocial: Grandmother’s view that she will grow out of it
Mother’s fear after searching online and fear of overreacting
ice: Idea: grandmother thinks it is normal; mother fears it is “something”
Concern: a tumour; being thought silly
Expectation: to know whether it matters

playbook.diagnosis: “The white look in the photos is a warning sign that the eye specialists need to check quickly, to rule out a problem at the back of the eye, including a rare tumour. The turning eye also needs checking so it doesn’t become lazy.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Normally a camera flash lights up the back of the eye and it looks red, like a red glow. If one eye looks white, something is stopping the light reaching or reflecting from the back of that eye, and we need specialists to find out what.”

management.reflectIce: “Your mum’s right that lots of squints are harmless, but you were right that the white in the photos is different. That’s exactly why we act on it today.”
management.psychosocial: Credit the mother, offer someone to come with her, give her words for the family, and plan around transport.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face red reflex, corneal light reflex and cover test today
Same-day call to ophthalmology: immediate if new squint with loss of red reflex (NICE NG127); otherwise suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12)
Squint and amblyopia assessed by the eye team; bring the photos
safetyNet: Headache, vomiting, unsteadiness, drowsiness, a red or painful eye: same day
Ring if no appointment within a few days; practice checks she was seen

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you act on a parent’s photo of a white pupil. Candidates often focus on the squint, reassure, and forget that the red reflex cannot be checked on video.

items.fail: Reassuring that she will grow out of the squint.
items.why: A persisting squint in a toddler risks amblyopia and can be the first sign of eye disease, including retinoblastoma.
items.fix: Refer the squint for orthoptic and ophthalmology assessment.

items.fail: Not asking to see the photographs.
items.why: The photos are the key evidence of leukocoria and help the specialists.
items.fix: “Can you show me the photo, or send it to the practice?”

items.why: NICE NG127: new squint with loss of the red reflex → immediate referral. NICE NG12: absent fundal reflex → suspected cancer pathway referral. A routine referral or review in months is unsafe.
items.fix: Check the reflex face to face today and phone ophthalmology to agree the route.

items.fail: Accepting that the red reflex cannot be examined on video and moving on.
items.why: An essential examination that cannot be done remotely must be arranged, not skipped.
items.fix: Bring her in the same day, and refer on the history even if the reflex looks equivocal.

items.fail: Saying “cancer” bluntly, or avoiding any mention of why it is urgent.
items.why: Either panic or unexplained urgency damages trust and engagement.
items.fix: Name the rare serious cause calmly, with the common treatable causes and the good outcome of early treatment.

items.fail: No plan to confirm the appointment happens.
items.why: Referral safety-netting is expected of the referring GP.
items.fix: “If you haven’t heard in a few days, ring me, and we’ll check she was seen.”

timeMap.d: Hear both problems: the intermittent squint and the white reflex in photos. Agree to go through both.
See the photos. Onset and pattern of the squint, vision, headache, vomiting, unsteadiness, eye pain or redness, family history.
Fear of a tumour after searching online; feeling silly because the family dismissed it. Validate her.
Leukocoria must be ruled out quickly; retinoblastoma named calmly with the good outlook; amblyopia risk from the squint.
Face-to-face red reflex today; call ophthalmology; NG127 or NICE NG12 route; bring photos; teach-back; chase the appointment; safety-net.

wordPics.fail: Agrees she will grow out of it or plans to review in a few months; never asks to see the photos; says the red reflex cannot be checked on video and stops there; no referral.
wordPics.pass: Recognises leukocoria as a red flag, arranges a red reflex check, refers to ophthalmology urgently and refers the squint, with a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: looks at the photos; knows the NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway for an absent fundal reflex and the NG127 immediate route for a new squint with loss of the red reflex; phones ophthalmology the same day; names retinoblastoma honestly with its good prognosis; supports the mother against family pressure; owns and chases the referral.

avoid.dont: “Lots of toddlers’ eyes wander. Let’s see how she is in a few months.”
avoid.instead: “The white reflex in the photos is something we always check quickly, and the squint needs the eye team too.”
avoid.why: Watchful waiting risks delaying a retinoblastoma diagnosis and missing the window for amblyopia treatment.

avoid.dont: “Flash photos are unreliable, I wouldn’t worry.”
avoid.instead: “Photos are often how this is first spotted. Can you show me?”
avoid.why: A parental report of leukocoria is a recognised presentation and should be acted on.

avoid.dont: “This could be eye cancer.” (said first, with no context)
avoid.instead: “Most causes are treatable eye conditions, but a rare tumour must be ruled out, so we check quickly.”
avoid.why: Honesty with context keeps a frightened parent engaged without causing panic.

I know that’s a frightening word to hear. I’m not saying she has it. I’m saying it needs to be ruled out quickly, and if it were found, it’s one of the childhood cancers that’s treated most successfully when it’s caught early. Checking quickly is the careful thing to do.
SCA_MODELS.why: Responds to distress with honesty and hope

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. And the turning eye?

The squint needs the specialists too. If an eye keeps turning, the brain can start ignoring it and it becomes a lazy eye, which is much easier to treat when she’s young. So “she’ll grow out of it” isn’t safe for Aria. The same eye team can look at both.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains amblyopia risk and why the squint needs referral

SCA_MODELS.text: I can’t check the red reflex properly over video, so I’d like to see her in person today, in a dim room with my ophthalmoscope. I’ll also phone the eye doctors at the hospital today. If the reflex is missing in that eye with the squint, they’ll want to see her within hours. Otherwise I’ll send an urgent referral on the fast-track pathway for suspected eye cancer, which means an appointment within two weeks. Either way, the referral goes today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Face-to-face red reflex, same-day ophthalmology discussion, NG127 immediate or NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway

SCA_MODELS.text: Today? Yes, I can bring her this afternoon.
Good, we’ll book a time this afternoon. Please bring the photos on your phone, because the specialists find them helpful. Would it help to have someone with you?
I’ll see who can come with me.
Good. Is there anything you’d like me to say differently to your mum? Some families find it helps to hear that the doctor asked for this, not that you overreacted.
Yes. I’ll tell her the doctor said it needs checking.
Can you tell me in your own words what we’ve agreed, so I know I’ve explained it well?
Bring her in this afternoon to check the red reflex and bring the photos. You’ll ring the eye doctors today, and she’ll be seen either very quickly or within two weeks. The squint gets checked too.

That’s exactly right. If you haven’t heard about the eye appointment within a few days, ring me and I’ll chase it. Before then, if she gets headaches, morning vomiting, becomes unsteady or drowsy, or the eye becomes red, painful or looks bigger, call us straight away or take her to A&E. I’ll also check with the hospital that she was seen.
SCA_MODELS.why: Timed follow-up, specific safety-net and ownership of the referral

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [2] NICE NG127 Suspected neurological conditions: recognition and referral (2019), children: new-onset squint · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [3] NHS Newborn and Infant Physical Examination (NIPE) screening programme: eye examination at birth and 6 to 8 weeks · [4] UK National Screening Committee: child vision screening (orthoptist-led, age 4 to 5)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A white pupil in flash photographs (leukocoria) in a toddler is a retinoblastoma warning sign until an eye specialist says otherwise. Take the mother’s observation seriously, look at the photos, arrange for the red reflex to be checked face to face, and refer to ophthalmology: an absent fundal reflex needs a suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12), and a new squint with loss of the red reflex needs an immediate referral (NG127). The squint needs specialist assessment in its own right because of the amblyopia risk. “She’ll grow out of it” is not safe advice here.

points.t: A white, pale or “cat’s eye” reflection in one pupil on flash photos, or an absent or abnormal red reflex on examination, can be caused by retinoblastoma, congenital cataract, Coats’ disease or other serious eye disease. Parents often notice it in photos first. The report alone is enough to act on.

NICE NG12 [1]: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral to ophthalmology for retinoblastoma in a child with an absent fundal (“red”) reflex. NICE NG12 now says “fundal” reflex because the normal reflex can look a different colour in children with darker skin.

points.h: NG127: squint plus loss of red reflex
points.t: NICE NG127 [2]: refer immediately to ophthalmology a child with a new-onset squint together with loss of the fundal (“red”) reflex in one or both eyes (seen within a few hours). It can signal retinoblastoma, other progressive eye disease or raised intracranial pressure. A new squint with headache, vomiting or ataxia needs immediate referral to acute paediatrics.

A persisting squint in a toddler is not something to wait on: the brain can suppress the turning eye and amblyopia (“lazy eye”) develops, which responds best to early glasses, patching or other treatment. In UK practice any squint beyond early infancy (about 3 months of age) is referred for orthoptic and ophthalmology assessment. A squint can also be the first sign of poor vision in that eye, including from retinoblastoma.

Face to face: red reflex of each eye separately and then both together from about an arm’s length in a dim room, comparing colour, brightness and symmetry; corneal light reflex and cover test; fixing and following; eyelids and pupils. On video: look at the photos, watch for the turn, and ask about vision, headache, vomiting and unsteadiness.

The red reflex is checked at the newborn and 6 to 8 week NIPE examinations [3], and orthoptist-led vision screening happens at 4 to 5 years [4]. A normal baby check does not rule out later disease, so a new parental concern overrides earlier reassurance.

Validate the mother’s instinct, explain honestly that the white reflex is the reason for urgency, say that most causes are not cancer but that this must be checked quickly, and avoid both false reassurance and frightening language. Confirm she knows when and where Aria will be seen.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start by video; heard both concerns; named the squint and the white reflex as separate items.
Family pressure (“she’ll grow out of it”), who can support the mother, practical barriers to attending today.
Picked up “white, not red” in photos and “am I being daft” and explored both.
Idea (grandmother: normal), concern (a tumour after searching online, fear of overreacting), expectation (to know if it matters).
Asked to see the photos; arranged face-to-face red reflex, corneal light reflex and cover test, fixation and following.
Retinoblastoma, congenital cataract and other retinal disease versus benign squint; amblyopia risk.
Asked about headache, vomiting, unsteadiness, drowsiness, eye pain or redness, reduced vision and family history.
Named leukocoria as a warning sign needing urgent specialist eye assessment; explained the squint risk.
Same-day phone call to ophthalmology; NG127 immediate if new squint with loss of red reflex, otherwise NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway referral; squint assessed by the same team.
Supported the mother, offered support for attending, helped her explain the plan to the family.
Teach-back; chase if no appointment in a few days; red flags for same-day review; practice confirms attendance.

social.t: Relatives saying “she’ll grow out of it” can make a parent doubt herself. Give her words to use at home and credit her for noticing.
Urgent eye appointments may be at a specialist centre some distance away. Ask about transport, childcare and work, and signpost support.

legal.t: A person with parental responsibility consents to examination and referral for a 2-year-old. Record who attended and what was agreed.
If an essential examination such as the red reflex cannot be done on video, arrange it face to face promptly rather than deferring the decision.

professional.t: Safety-net properly: confirm the referral was received and the child was seen. Missed or delayed suspected cancer referrals in children are a recognised source of harm.
NICE NG12 asks clinicians to take persistent parental concern seriously and consider referral. Here there is a specific red flag as well.

community.t: The Childhood Eye Cancer Trust (CHECT) gives family information on retinoblastoma. Health visitors can support follow-up and later orthoptic care.

redFlags: White or absent red reflex, including in flash photos
New squint with loss of the red reflex (NG127: immediate referral)
New squint with headache, vomiting or unsteadiness (immediate paediatric referral)
Reduced vision, a painful red eye or a change in eye size
psychosocial: Grandmother’s view that she will grow out of it
Mother’s fear after searching online and fear of overreacting
ice: Idea: grandmother thinks it is normal; mother fears it is “something”
Concern: a tumour; being thought silly
Expectation: to know whether it matters

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “The white look in the photos is a warning sign that the eye specialists need to check quickly, to rule out a problem at the back of the eye, including a rare tumour. The turning eye also needs checking so it doesn’t become lazy.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Normally a camera flash lights up the back of the eye and it looks red, like a red glow. If one eye looks white, something is stopping the light reaching or reflecting from the back of that eye, and we need specialists to find out what.”

management.reflectIce: “Your mum’s right that lots of squints are harmless, but you were right that the white in the photos is different. That’s exactly why we act on it today.”
management.psychosocial: Credit the mother, offer someone to come with her, give her words for the family, and plan around transport.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face red reflex, corneal light reflex and cover test today
Same-day call to ophthalmology: immediate if new squint with loss of red reflex (NICE NG127); otherwise suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12)
Squint and amblyopia assessed by the eye team; bring the photos
safetyNet: Headache, vomiting, unsteadiness, drowsiness, a red or painful eye: same day
Ring if no appointment within a few days; practice checks she was seen

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you act on a parent’s photo of a white pupil. Candidates often focus on the squint, reassure, and forget that the red reflex cannot be checked on video.

items.fail: Reassuring that she will grow out of the squint.
items.why: A persisting squint in a toddler risks amblyopia and can be the first sign of eye disease, including retinoblastoma.
items.fix: Refer the squint for orthoptic and ophthalmology assessment.

items.fail: Not asking to see the photographs.
items.why: The photos are the key evidence of leukocoria and help the specialists.
items.fix: “Can you show me the photo, or send it to the practice?”

items.why: NICE NG127: new squint with loss of the red reflex → immediate referral. NICE NG12: absent fundal reflex → suspected cancer pathway referral. A routine referral or review in months is unsafe.
items.fix: Check the reflex face to face today and phone ophthalmology to agree the route.

items.fail: Accepting that the red reflex cannot be examined on video and moving on.
items.why: An essential examination that cannot be done remotely must be arranged, not skipped.
items.fix: Bring her in the same day, and refer on the history even if the reflex looks equivocal.

items.fail: Saying “cancer” bluntly, or avoiding any mention of why it is urgent.
items.why: Either panic or unexplained urgency damages trust and engagement.
items.fix: Name the rare serious cause calmly, with the common treatable causes and the good outcome of early treatment.

items.fail: No plan to confirm the appointment happens.
items.why: Referral safety-netting is expected of the referring GP.
items.fix: “If you haven’t heard in a few days, ring me, and we’ll check she was seen.”
